facts.claim: "I Guess" by Saint Levant and Playyard was released as a single on December 12, 2022. It runs 2:38 and is credited to 2048 LLC.
Playyard is the artist and producer Henry Morris, who is Saint Levant's college friend (Saint Levant's real name is Marwan Abdelhamid).
The track was produced by Henry Morris and Marwan Abdelhamid (Saint Levant). It uses live instrumentation, with a lead guitar riff and a drum beat that comes in later in the song.
Morris and Abdelhamid wrote the bass line first. They then sent it to Abdelhamid's father, who suggested sampling Timbaland and Elton John's 2007 collaboration "2 Man Show."
Rolling Stone describes the song as sensual and Brent Faiyaz-like. It is sung from the perspective of a man who questions whether his lover really knows him. Saint Levant called it a bedroom song.
Playyard sings the opening hook. Saint Levant follows with his deep vocal register and multilingual delivery. The music video shows the two in record stores, on metro cars and performing on stage.
The song refers to Saint Levant leaving home for the US at 17, in the line about being 17 when he left home.
The song came out shortly after Saint Levant's viral trilingual (English, French, Arabic) track "Very Few Friends" in November 2022.

Saint Levant is a Palestinian singer-songwriter and rapper. He was born Marwan Abdelhamid on October 6, 2000, in Jerusalem, and is based in California. His stage name puns on Yves Saint Laurent and the Levant region.

Saint Levant began listening to Arab hip-hop artists such as Shabjdeed and Marwan Moussa in his teens. Rolling Stone says his lyrics try to normalize taboo discussions of sex and mental health in the Middle East and North Africa.

research.lineage: The song sits in a multilingual, genre-blending Palestinian diaspora hip-hop and R&B scene, influenced by Arab hip-hop artists like Shabjdeed and Marwan Moussa.

draft:
The most telling moment in **I Guess** comes in Arabic. Saint Levant switches out of English to tell a lover, again and again, to take it easy and that he understands her. Then he raises the stakes and swears it on his mother's life. In the English verses he is sarcastic and guarded. When he reaches for his mother tongue, the defenses drop and he simply pleads to be believed.

The hook, which Playyard sings, sets up the hurt. Someone who left is out "living it up" and still thinking of the two of them in the club. She once said it was never enough. The reply is a shrug with a bruise under it: "I guess, that I'on't know shit." It's pride talking, conceding the argument so he doesn't have to admit how much it stings. Rolling Stone describes the song as a man questioning whether his lover really knows him. Saint Levant called it a bedroom song, and the verses are frank about desire. But the ache keeps showing through. He says he has a lot on his mind and needs to share the pain. Twice he says he doesn't think she really wants him, and each time he leaves a door open after it.

Then comes the line that widens the frame: "I was 17 when I left home." That's Saint Levant's own story. He was born in Jerusalem and moved to the U.S. at 17, and he pictures himself setting out in Timberlands and headphones. All of a sudden the doubt about being known runs deeper than one relationship. Here is someone far from where he started, wondering if anyone has the full picture.

The track itself is spare and close. A synth bass and a dry drum machine with a firm snare hold a laid-back, unhurried groove. A short plucked melodic figure repeats on top, and Saint Levant and Playyard (producer Henry Morris, his college friend) built it around a lead guitar riff. Nothing is soaked in reverb, so the rapping sounds conversational, almost spoken across a pillow. Morris and Saint Levant wrote the bass line first. Saint Levant's father then suggested sampling Timbaland and Elton John's "2 Man Show," and the closing refrain about having been around the world takes its shape from there, two friends making the most of a small setup.

It's easy to see why Rolling Stone heard Brent Faiyaz in it. The song also comes from a teenager who grew up on Arab rappers like Shabjdeed and Marwan Moussa. That background helps explain why the frankness about sex and pain doesn't seem forced. He's speaking plainly about the things that usually go unsaid.

What sticks is how the song flips between two languages, a shrug in English and an oath in Arabic, so you can hear how badly he needs to be understood.
